Bomb-disposal robot and drone with explosives discovered at Germany's Leipzig airport

In Germany, a drone carrying an explosive device was discovered and defused on the tarmac at Leipzig Airport. A second flying object then struck a cargo plane, causing minor damage. Air traffic was suspended for two hours. A Russian connection is being suggested. The interior minister describes a new dimension of threat to Germany. Story by Morgan Ayre.

corpus.title: Explosive drone forces shutdown at major German airport serving NATO, Ukraine flights
corpus.signal_text:
A drone carrying explosives was found near a Ukrainian plane at Germany's Leipzig/Halle Airport late Tuesday, prompting officials to warn the incident represented "a new quality of danger," authorities said Wednesday.
The discovery temporarily shut down both runways at the major European freight hub and forced several flights to divert to other airports, according to The Associated Press.
Another flying object was spotted nearby shortly before midnight and several flights, including one passenger plane, were then diverted to other airports.
JETBLUE FLIGHT REPORTS DRONE STRIKE DURING APPROACH TO NEW YORK AIRPORT: FAA
German police launched a large response and opened an investigation into the two incidents.
Police said an airport worker found the first explosive drone near the airport's south runway with "an unknown explosive device."
An explosives disposal robot was deployed to examine the device before authorities removed its detonator.
The plane, bearing the blue and yellow colors of the Ukrainian flag, displayed the English-language slogan, "Be Brave Like Kherson," a tribute to the southern Ukrainian region, Deutsche Welle reported.
In the second incident, an unidentified flying object collided with a cargo aircraft that had aborted its landing at Leipzig/Halle Airport because of the runway closure.

The aircraft diverted to Hannover Airport, about 125 miles north-west of Leipzig, where officials found minor damage, according to The Associated Press.
German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt said the discovery of the first drone marked a significant escalation.
"Drone sightings, drone threats, including in a hybrid context, are something we know from the past," he said. "That a drone armed with explosives is at an airport is a new threat scenario."
Dobrindt also described the incident as "a hybrid attack scenario."
He said questions about the type of explosives used, the drone's origin and who was responsible remained under investigation.
"All the speculation that is currently going on about the explosives, the construction, the question of the drone, the origin and, of course, who is behind it, is now part of the investigation," Dobrindt said.
"What is happening now also shows that the assessment made months ago — that we are dealing with a high level of danger — was justified."

Drone With Detonator Found Near Ukrainian Plane at Leipzig Airport

German authorities found a drone carrying a package with a detonator near a Ukrainian Antonov cargo plane at Leipzig/Halle Airport shortly before midnight on Tuesday, Aug. 5, Bild reported. Investigators classified the device as a potential explosive. The airport was shut down for nearly two hours while bomb disposal teams responded. A cargo plane that had to abort landing later collided with an unknown object about 6 km from the airport. Police have not ruled out sabotage.

corpus.signal_text:
Drone with explosives found at German airport, official sees 'new quality' of threat
BERLIN — A drone with explosives was found at Germany's Leipzig/Halle Airport and the device was defused, authorities said Wednesday, in an incident that the country's top security official said posed a "new quality of danger."
Both the runways at the major freight hub were closed and several flights, including one passenger plane, were diverted to other airports after a flying object was sighted nearby shortly before midnight Tuesday. An anti-explosives robot was deployed to check an object near the south runway.
Regional police and prosecutors later said an airport employee discovered a drone near the airport's south runway with "an unknown explosive device," and the object was examined by police. They removed its detonator.
That the drone was carrying explosives "is a new quality of danger," German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt told reporters at the airport after interrupting his vacation to travel to the scene.
"Drone sightings, drone threats including in a hybrid context, are something we know from the past," he added. "That a drone armed with explosives is at an airport is a new threat scenario."
Dobrindt described what happened as "a hybrid attack scenario," but didn't offer more details of authorities' assessment or specify who might be responsible.
He said questions about details of the explosives, the origin of the drone and who was behind the incident were a matter for the ongoing investigation.
The regional interior minister of Saxony state, Armin Schuster, said authorities were looking for parts of a possible second drone.
Police and prosecutors said an apparent second flying object collided with a freight airplane after it aborted a landing at Leipzig/Halle because the runway was closed. The plane flew to another German airport, Hannover, about 200 kilometers (125 miles) to the northwest, where officials found slight damage.
The north runway at Leipzig/Halle was reopened after about two hours. The south runway was scheduled to be out of action for maintenance on Wednesday. Authorities said there was no danger to passengers or airport employees, and flights weren't affected during the day.
Photos from the scene showed police technicians with an explosives-disposal robot near a Ukrainian plane. The airport is a leading cargo hub and the planes located there include Ukrainian Antonov transport aircraft.

corpus.title: Germany Probes 'Hybrid Attack' At Leipzig Airport After Explosive Drone Found Near Ukrainian Plane
corpus.signal_text:
German authorities are investigating two "very serious security incidents" at the Leipzig/Halle airport that temporarily suspended and diverted flights, raising suspicions of Russian involvement following similar incidents in recent years.
The Leipzig Police Directorate said in a statement that late on August 4, "an unidentified flying object" was sighted near the airport, prompting the diversion of several aircraft, including a passenger plane, to other airports.
A drone carrying a "suspicious object" was also discovered in the vicinity of one of the two main runways.
The Dresden Public Prosecutor's Office and the Saxony State Criminal Police Office, which are leading the investigation, said the drone discovered on the runway was carrying "an unknown explosive device."
"With the support of the Federal Police and a bomb disposal robot, the object was examined. The Federal Police's IED unit removed the detonator," it said.
Operations on the airport's north runway resumed early on August 5, but the south runway, where the object on the ground was found, remains closed as police investigate, authorities said.
"The incidents at Leipzig Airport constitute a very serious security incident," Minister of State for the Interior Armin Schuster said in a separate statement.
Several German media outlets, including Bild, reported that the drone was discovered in the immediate vicinity of a Ukrainian An-124 cargo aircraft.
Video footage broadcast by several German media outlets showed the plane on the runway with emergency vehicles next to it.
German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt cut his summer break short and returned to the country to address the incident. He said the armed drone found was a hybrid attack which opened a "new level of danger."
Addressing journalists who had gathered at the airport, Dobrindt said that people behind the incident would need to have a high level of technical expertise and experience in dealing with explosives. This spoke against "an amateurish approach," Dobrindt said.
"We are dealing here with a professional hybrid threat scenario," he added.
In another incident at the same airport on August 5, a DHL cargo aircraft reportedly collided midair with an unknown object shortly after takeoff from Leipzig, prompting an immediate unscheduled landing in Hanover.
The Leipzig/Halle airport is a major logistical hub for DHL, a German-owned international shipping giant.

corpus.title: Today in Germany: A roundup of the latest news on Thursday
corpus.signal_text:
Thursday's top story: Explosive drone at German airport 'a new level of danger': minister
German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt has described the discovery of an explosive-laden drone at Leipzig-Halle Airport as a “professional hybrid threat scenario” that represents a new level of danger.
Authorities found, defused and later destroyed the drone after it was discovered near a Ukrainian-flagged cargo aircraft at the airport.
Dobrindt said investigators were examining the drone’s construction, the explosives used, its origin and any individuals or organisations potentially responsible. He stressed that the incident did not appear to be the work of amateurs and suggested that foreign actors could be among the possible sources of the threat, although investigations remain ongoing.
The discovery caused significant disruption at the airport, forcing the diversion of numerous flights.
In a separate incident, an aircraft that had aborted its landing reportedly collided with an unidentified object several kilometres away but was able to land safely.
Leipzig-Halle Airport is strategically important, serving military transport operations for Germany and its NATO allies, while also functioning as a base for Ukraine’s Antonov Airlines.

Berlin marks 65th anniversary of Wall construction with public installation
Berlin will commemorate the 65th anniversary of the beginning of the Berlin Wall’s construction with a temporary installation and open-air exhibition near the Brandenburg Gate.
Organised by the Berlin Wall Foundation, the commemorations will run from August 13th to 16th.
A 30-metre-long, almost three-metre-high structure designed to resemble the Berlin Wall will be erected close to the Brandenburg Gate. Alongside it, the exhibition Mauerblicke: Berlin 1961–1990 will use historical photographs to document the progressive closure of the city and the experiences of Berliners living under division.
Photo: picture alliance/dpa | Britta Pedersen
The anniversary programme will also include discussions with eyewitnesses, guided tours, concerts and readings across the city.
Full details are due to be announced on August 12th, one day before the anniversary of August 13th, 1961, when the East German government sealed the border with West Berlin.
